title: The Lens Lab
summary: Light a lantern with a lens, dial a lens pair, fire a projector shot, race a beam through two lenses and vanish a lens.
subject: physics
ncertRef: Section 9.5, Refraction at spherical surfaces and by lenses
concepts: Power of a lens in dioptres
Lenses in contact add their powers
learningOutcome: The student can use 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ + 1/R₂), 1/v − 1/u = 1/f, P = 1/f for lenses in contact, chain two lenses, and say how a liquid changes a lens’s focal length.

levels.title: Light the lantern
levels.adds: Baseline: the lens-maker’s formula fixes the focal length from n and the radii, so dial the radius that puts the focus on the lantern (Ex 9.7, Example 9.7).
hints: 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ + 1/R₂) for a double-convex lens; a flat face counts as 1/R = 0.
If one radius is fixed, find 1/R₂ = 1/((n − 1)f) − 1/R₁ and invert it.

levels.title: The power pair
levels.adds: New idea: lenses in contact add their powers, P = 1/f in dioptres with f in metres; dial the back lens to make the pair you need (Ex 9.10).
hints: Convert to dioptres: P = 100/f with f in cm. Converging is positive, diverging negative.
The pair’s power is P₁ + P₂, so the back lens is P₂ = target − P₁.
Do not add the focal lengths: add the powers.

levels.title: The projector shot
levels.adds: Apply it: with the slide and the screen D apart, u + v = D and v = mu fix the lens position and its focal length together (Ex 9.19, 9.9).
hints: For a magnification m the image distance is v = mu, and u + v = D.
Dial that focal length and stand the lens u from the slide.

levels.title: Test chamber 09
levels.adds: New idea: the image from lens 1 is the object for lens 2, even when it lies beyond lens 2 as a virtual object (Ex 9.20, Example 9.8).
hints: Use lens 1 alone: v₁ = u₁f₁/(u₁ − f₁). A flash charge shows it.
The distance from lens 2 to that image is v₁ − s; if the image is beyond lens 2 the object is virtual and u₂ is positive.
Apply 1/v₂ = 1/f₂ + 1/u₂ for lens 2, and add s to v₂ to place the screen.

levels.title: The magician’s tank
levels.adds: New idea: in a liquid 1/f′ ∝ (n_glass/n_liquid − 1); equal indices make the lens vanish and a denser liquid makes it diverge (Example 9.6, 9.7).
hints: From the radii and f in air, find the glass: n = 1 + R/(2f).
f′/f = (n_g − 1)/(n_g/n_l − 1). If n_l equals n_g the focal length is infinite.
Above n_g the bracket is negative, so the lens diverges.

levels.title: One curved face
levels.adds: New: one curved face: n₂/v − n₁/u = (n₂ − n₁)/R; dial the radius that focuses the light on the sensor inside the rod (Section 9.5.1; Example 9.5).
hints: Light goes from air (n₁ = 1) into glass (n₂ = 1.5) or water (4/3).
Put in u (negative, the lamp is in front) and v, the depth of the sensor.
A negative R means the face curves the other way: concave.

misconceptions: A lens always converges light, whatever surrounds it
The focal length of two lenses in contact is the sum of their focal lengths
Light needs a real object before the second lens can bend it
